definition: General agreement among most or all members of a group.
example: After an hour of debate, the hiking club reached a consensus to take the shorter trail.
nuance: Consensus is broad shared agreement, not necessarily unanimity, and it never describes a single person's opinion.
prompt: A neighborhood committee must decide what to plant in the shared garden.
options: After hearing every proposal, the committee reached a consensus to plant tomatoes and herbs.
The committee took a consensus by counting every household living on the block.
The consensus was that half the members wanted roses while the other half refused to plant anything.
The chairwoman announced her personal consensus without asking anyone else in the room.
reasons: The members arrived at a broadly shared decision together, which is what the word names.
Counting residents is a census; this word refers to agreement, not a headcount.
An even split with no shared view is a deadlock, the opposite of general agreement.
One person's private opinion cannot be agreement among a group.

practice.prompt: Scientists from several labs compare their measurements of how fast a glacier is melting.
options: One researcher reached a consensus with herself after rechecking her own spreadsheet.
The lead scientist imposed a consensus by forbidding anyone to publish a different number.
When the data from all five labs matched, a consensus formed around the melting rate.
Each lab published a different rate, so the consensus among them was complete disagreement.
reasons: Agreement of this kind requires a group; one person confirming her work does not qualify.
Silencing others by order produces obedience, not agreement the group genuinely shares.
Independent researchers converging on the same conclusion is broad agreement among experts.
Total disagreement is the absence of shared agreement, not a kind of it.
